title: SAD-Flower: Safe, Admissible, Dynamically Consistent Planning
one_liner: Flow-matching models generate robot trajectories by adding a virtual control layer that guarantees safety, stays within limits, and stays physically executable.
lead: Flow matching is a method where a neural network learns to transform random noise into planned trajectories by following smooth paths in number-space. The problem: these paths can violate hard rules like collision bounds or motor limits, and they can predict motion that breaks the laws of physics. SAD-Flower fixes this by wrapping the flow matcher in a virtual control layer that rewrites the trajectory on the fly, ensuring safety, obedience to constraints, and physical consistency—without retraining.

problem.h2: Flow Matching Generates Paths That Break Robot Rules
paras: A flow matcher is a neural network that learns to generate robot movement plans (sequences of positions and motor commands over time) by training on good trajectory examples. At test time, you feed it a random starting point and it nudges it step by step toward realistic, useful motion.

The catch: there are three rules these trajectories must obey in the real world. First, safety constraints—the robot must not hit walls or obstacles. Second, action constraints—the motor commands must stay within safe power and torque limits. Third, dynamic consistency—the predicted motion must follow the actual laws of physics that govern the robot, so the plan is actually executable when sent to the real machine.

Naive flow matching has no way to guarantee any of these three rules at test time. It can violate collision bounds, exceed motor limits, and produce motion that contradicts physics. Rejection sampling—generate many trajectories and discard the broken ones—wastes huge computation and often fails on tight constraints.

callout.html: Wrap the flow matcher in a virtual control layer that resets the trajectory to obey safety, motor, and physics rules on every step.

steps.text: Flow matcher generates a raw path by smoothly deforming random noise.
For every position and command in the path, measure if it breaks a rule.
Pose rule-fixing as an optimization: nudge the flow path as little as possible while obeying all constraints.
Use techniques from control theory (barrier functions) to compute the legal adjustments at each step.
The modified path now guarantees safety, motor obedience, and physics consistency without retraining.

paras: The flow matcher itself is unchanged. Instead, SAD-Flower adds a control layer that rewrites the trajectory in real time at test time. It takes the raw flow output and feeds it through a constraint-satisfaction optimizer before handing it to the robot. This virtual control input acts like an invisible hand that gently pushes the trajectory toward legality without breaking the learned motion patterns.

hidden.h2: The Hidden Quantity: Constraint Violation Margin
hidden.name: Constraint violation margin at each step
paras: SAD-Flower measures how close the trajectory is to breaking each rule at each time step. For safety: the distance to the nearest obstacle. For motors: how much headroom remains before torque or power limits. For physics: whether the predicted motion matches what the laws of motion dictate—if the arm says it will swing down with a certain acceleration, does that match gravity and the arm's mass? If not, the trajectory is dynamically inconsistent and will fail on the real robot. Each of these is a number—how much illegal we are right now.

The paper uses control-theoretic tools (Barrier Functions for state and action constraints, Lyapunov Functions for physics) to track these margins. When a margin goes negative (rule broken), the optimizer pulls it back to zero. The control layer continuously estimates and enforces these margins from the learned flow model without ever retraining it.

heat.caption: Darker means closer to violating that constraint at that time step; highlights mark the margins that trigger correction.

reads.html: At each moment in the robot's motion, the control layer checks: am I about to hit something? Am I about to exceed my motor limits? Am I about to move in a way physics forbids? Each check is a number. If any number is negative, the optimizer adjusts the path.

SAD-Flower formulates constraints as Control Barrier Functions for state safety and action admissibility, and Control Lyapunov Functions for dynamic consistency. The flow model prediction is treated as a virtual control input. At test time, a quadratic program enforces non-negative margins on all three constraints across the full trajectory horizon.

mechanism.h2: Why It Works: Hijack the Flow As a Controllable System
paras: The core insight: instead of asking the flow matcher to learn constraint satisfaction (which requires retraining), treat the flow model as an existing dynamical system with a secret control input baked in. The flow model predicts: given where I am now, here is my next move. SAD-Flower adds a second question: given where I am now, here is my next move from the learned flow, but what adjustment do I need to apply so that adjustment respects all three rules?

Here is the real mechanism. The flow matcher has already learned realistic motion from data. At test time, the control layer reformulates the optimization as: minimize how much you change the flow's suggestion, subject to three hard constraints. This is a quadratic program—fast to solve. The constraints themselves come from control theory: barrier functions keep you away from bad states (collisions, motor overload), and Lyapunov functions ensure the dynamics obey physics. The solution is the smallest tweak to the flow that passes all three tests, applied every single step.

Why this works without retraining: the control layer does not retrain the flow matcher. It only solves an optimization at each step. The flow model's learned patterns are preserved. The constraints are enforced formally, not learned approximately. And because control theory provides a direct mechanism—not a classifier or a learned guidance—the method carries formal guarantees. Unseen constraints at test time are handled the same way: the barrier functions adapt to new bounds without any retraining.

stages.s: Measure constraint margins at each time step
Pose optimization: least change to flow, all margins non-negative
Solve via quadratic program using barrier functions

math.h2: The Equation: Minimize Change, Enforce Constraints
math.words: At each time step, find the smallest adjustment to the flow's prediction such that the safety margin stays non-negative, the motor margin stays non-negative, and the physics margin stays non-negative.
math.equation: min_{delta} ||delta||^2  subject to  h_s(x + delta) >= 0,  h_a(u + delta_u) >= 0,  h_p(dynamics) >= 0
symbols: adjustment to the position or command predicted by flow
squared size of that adjustment—keep it small
barrier function measuring distance to collision (safety)
barrier function measuring distance to motor limits (admissibility)
function measuring alignment with physics laws (dynamic consistency)
current predicted position from flow matcher
current predicted motor command from flow matcher

worked.title: A tiny worked example
lines: Flow matcher predicts: next position = 5.0, next motor command = 12.0.
Safety check: distance to nearest wall = 0.3 (positive, safe).
Motor check: available torque headroom = 2.0 (positive, in limit).
Physics check: predicted acceleration matches laws = 0.1 (positive, consistent).
All three margins are non-negative. Adjustment delta = 0. Return flow prediction unchanged.
Different example: flow predicts next motor command = 15.0, but limit is 14.5.
Optimizer finds: delta_u = -0.6 reduces command to 14.4.
Safety and physics margins still non-negative. Return adjusted trajectory.

math.note: The optimizer finds the tiniest push to the flow's output that makes all three constraint barriers non-negative, preserving the learned motion while enforcing formal safety.

charts.note: Raw flow matcher violates multiple rules frequently on test tasks.

charts.note: Constraint layer ensures all three rules pass across Maze2d, Hopper, Walker, and Block Stacking tasks.

items.html: If the task goal and a safety constraint truly conflict (e.g., goal requires entering a no-go zone), the optimizer cannot satisfy both. The method will obey the constraint and sacrifice the goal. This is correct behavior but may reduce task reward.

The control layer uses numerical integration to solve the dynamics. Too few integration steps introduce small violations and jerky motion. The paper shows this: with few steps the trajectory wiggles, violating smoothness. Enough steps fix it.

When test-time constraints become much stricter than training data (e.g., 70% taller constraint reduced to 50%), the optimizer must work harder to fit both safety and the task. Motion quality degrades, though constraint satisfaction holds.

When constraints are reasonable and independent, SAD-Flower consistently achieves perfect constraint satisfaction while maintaining plan quality. The method scales across different robot morphologies and tasks without retraining.

demo.h2: What a runnable demo should prove
paras: Build a simple robot task (e.g., a 2D maze or an arm reaching a target) where you can toggle hard constraints: an obstacle the arm must not hit, a motor torque limit, and a gravity law the arm obeys. Train a flow matcher on good trajectories from that task (unconstrained). At test time, try three methods: (1) raw flow matching (no constraint checking), (2) rejection sampling (generate 100 trajectories, keep only legal ones), (3) SAD-Flower (apply the control layer). Measure: percentage of trajectories that satisfy all three constraints, and average task success rate for the surviving plans.
demo.closing: The demo should make it impossible to miss: SAD-Flower returns a safe, in-limit, executable plan on the first try, while naive flow often breaks rules and rejection sampling wastes huge samples to fix a problem that control theory solves in one step.
